newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong eyes focused on post-Deng Beijing.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong eyes focused on post-Deng Beijing.

text.p: There were some grumbles about the disruption to television programming.
But most of Hong Kong spent hours glued to reports from Beijing which bumped the soap operas off the air to tell of the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
For nothwithstanding the matter-of-fact reaction in the British colony to Deng's passing, Hong Kong eyes are now focused north seeking reassurance of a smooth political succession.

With just 128 days to go until Britain hands Hong Kong over to a country many here fled, there is little Hong Kong fears more than a damaging power struggle breaking out in Beijing's alleyways of power.
"I think if I could use the analogy, Hong Kong is the flea on the end of the dog's tail," said academic David Newman, a senior lecturer at Hong Kong's Lingnan College.
"In most cases, in the terms of Chinese politics nobody will really worry too much about Hong Kong. But if things get uncertain in China, it's the tail that will bounce around the most on the dog."
Deng, 92, died in Beijing on Wednesday evening of complications from a lung infection and Parkinson's disease.
With him died his dream of witnessing the end of a century and a half of Chinese humilation at the hands of British occupiers. Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30.
It was Deng who led the negotiations to recover Hong Kong. He promised the wary populace that China would not seek to mould the fiercely capitalist territory to communism.

His "one country-two systems" formula, designed eventually to woo Taiwan, too, back to the fold, would give Hong Kong people considerable autonomy in running their affairs. Communist cadres, he pledged, would not be sent south to run vibrant Hong Kong.
No one here seriously expects Maoist hardliners to regain control in Beijing and seek to re-collectivise China.
But some fret about aspiring leaders taking a tougher line on Hong Kong affairs to head off accusations of weakness in the bitter closed-door battles for power and influence.
British Governor Chris Patten sought to allay Hong Kong anxieties on Sunday by extolling its strengths.

"I can't speculate any more successfully than the next man or woman about what is going to happen in China, or by extension what is going to happen here as a result of Mr Deng's death," he said on government radio's Letter from Hong Kong broadcast.
"But what we do know -- it's not speculation -- is what sort of place Hong Kong is.
"What we know is that it's a strong enough community to withstand almost anything which the history of the coming months and years may throw at it."

Newman, co-author of "Red Flag Over Hong Kong", which paints a bleak post-handover future of rigged elections and a government and judiciary answerable only to Beijing, said Deng's anointed successor Jiang Zemin was not very secure.
"He's got to demonstrate over the next six months that he's entitled to the position that was given to him by Deng Xiaoping," Newman told Reuters.

"Some of this will be involved in taking actions that demonstrate they (the leadership) are in control -- firing of missiles (at Taiwan), being hard on the U.S. in trade negotiations, taking a harder stance in Hong Kong.
"And at other times they will simply want to take a low-key approach to things, essentially retrench into themselves, assure themselves ... that they are in control."
"I think we are likely to be seeing both sorts of actions on the part of the mainland leaders," Newman said.
